lines.text: Why does Chicago teach its eighth graders about one police commander?
His name was Jon Burge. For two decades, detectives under his command on Chicago's South Side tortured confessions out of more than one hundred Black men.

Survivors described a hand-cranked box with two wires. Electric shock. Suffocation. Mock executions. In 1982, a jail doctor demanded, in writing, an investigation of the brutality. The letter reached the top — and nothing happened. For decades, complaints fell on deaf ears.

By the time the truth was official, the statute of limitations had run out. The torture could never be prosecuted. So federal prosecutors charged the only crime left — lying about it under oath. Four and a half years. He kept his police pension until the day he died.

In 2015, Chicago passed America's first municipal reparations for police violence — and put this story in its schools, so the city can never say it didn't know. Follow for the cases they don't teach you.
